content: Bowen's disease is a type of neoplastic skin condition that is classified as an early stage or intraepidermal form of squamous cell carcinoma. It was first described in 1912 by Dr. John T. Bowen, after whom the disease is named. Clinically, Bowen's disease typically manifests as a slowly enlarging, well-defined erythematous plaque. The lesion often has an irregular border and may exhibit surface crusting or scaling. While it can occur at any age in adults, it is rare in individuals under 30 years old and is most commonly diagnosed in patients over the age of 60. Women are disproportionately affected, accounting for 70-85% of cases. Approximately three-quarters of patients present with lesions on the lower legs, particularly in areas of skin that have been exposed to sunlight. However, the disease can occur on any part of the skin or mucosal surfaces, though it is uncommon on the palms or soles. The lesions are characterized by a persistent, progressive, non-elevated red scaly or crusted plaque. This is due to the presence of an intradermal carcinoma, which is potentially malignant. Histologically, atypical squamous cells proliferate throughout the entire thickness of the epidermis. Treatment options for Bowen's disease include freezing (cryotherapy), cauterization, or diathermy coagulation, all of which are often effective. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) and local chemotherapy with agents such as 5-fluorouracil are also commonly used and are sometimes preferred by clinicians over surgical excision. Bowen's disease must be distinguished from other conditions that cause papulosquamous or erythrodermic squamous rashes. Differential diagnoses include other dermatological conditions with similar clinical presentations. Histologically, Bowen's disease is equivalent to squamous cell carcinoma in situ. The tumor is confined entirely to the epidermis and does not invade the dermis. Under the microscope, the cells in Bowen's disease appear highly atypical and, in many cases, look more abnormal than the cells of some invasive squamous cell carcinomas. The degree of cellular atypia observed under the microscope is a key indicator of how the cells might behave if they were to invade other tissues. Because the abnormal cells in Bowen's disease remain confined to the epidermis and do not invade the dermis, the prognosis is significantly better than that of invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
